The writer incorporates a variety of sensory details—including sight, sound, smell, and touch—to make the settings feel tangible and real. For example, in the college dormitory, the narrator mentions the sound and physical sensation of "windows [that] rattled when trucks crossed the bridge." Later, the municipal pool is brought to life through its distinct smells ("chlorine, coffee, and damp wool"), visual details (a "painted blue whale," a "man in a red bathing cap," and the "red mark across his palm" left by a goggle strap), and tactile/temperature elements (an apartment that was "too hot," "wet tile," and stepping out into the rain before riding a bus with "fogged" windows). These details ground the narrative in a believable physical world.
